intro: Section 34.3 asks what disciplines outside medicine teach psychiatry. Its first half, built here, looks at behavior through evolution and animal study. Sociobiology asks why a behavior exists at all and reads competition, aggression, mating and altruism in terms of reproductive success. Identical twins raised apart test nature against nurture. Ethology, the study of animal behavior, brings imprinting, displacement activity, sign stimuli and the honeybee dance. Primate research shows what isolation and separation do to young monkeys and how peers can rehabilitate them, and laboratory work produced experimental neuroses, learned helplessness and drug-induced syndromes. The part ends with sensory deprivation and three ways to explain its effects. The second half of the section (34.3b) covers transcultural psychiatry.
objectives: Explain what sociobiology asks, define evolutionary fitness, and describe how the chapter applies competition, aggression, reproduction and altruism to psychiatric disorders.
Summarize the reared-apart twin findings on IQ, personality and behavior, including the correlations the chapter reports, and state their limits.
Define the key ethologic terms and match Lorenz, Tinbergen and von Frisch with their discoveries and the human links the chapter draws.
Contrast social isolation with separation in monkeys, describe Harlow's surrogate studies and Suomi's peer therapy, and explain how temperament and early stress interact.
Describe the main experimental disorders in animals (stress syndromes, learned helplessness, dominance, brain stimulation, drug-induced models) and what each was used to model.
Describe Hebb's sensory deprivation experiment, its effects, and the psychological, cognitive and physiologic theories offered to explain them.
